notes:
THE FIRST CHRISTIAN COMMUNITIES - STUDY NOTES

Note: this chapter is in Part 4, ‘The Formation of the Christian Community’. The topic is also looked at in Section C (World Religions), Section D (Moral Decision-making), Section F (Issues of Justice and Peace), Section G (Worship, Prayer and Ritual) and Section H (The Bible: Literature and Sacred Text).

KEY TERMS
- Community: a group of people who come together because they share certain beliefs or interests.
- Ekklesia: the term the New Testament communities used for themselves. For followers of the risen Jesus it came to mean the true community of God. Used widely in Acts and in Paul’s letters.
- Kehal Yahweh: the Jewish equivalent of Ekklesia - ‘the community of God’.
- Eschatological community: a community keeping the message of Jesus alive until the imminent (very soon) coming of the Kingdom of God.
- Fledgling community: a new, young community that is just starting out (used of Philippi).
- Radical faith: Christianity’s demands for love, sharing and unity, which were hard to live out (used of Corinth).
- Resurrection of the dead: belief that the dead will rise. Paul taught that if you do not believe in the resurrection of the dead, you do not believe in the resurrection of Jesus.
- Gentiles: non-Jews.
- Second coming: the return of Jesus at the end of time.

WHY PEOPLE FORM COMMUNITIES
- When people share an experience or interest, they naturally gather in groups to remember it, celebrate it and relive it.
- Examples: people who shared a wonderful holiday meet months later with photos and stories; sports lovers set up a club to train and play.
- In this way people connect, have fun, build friendships and sometimes form communities.
- Being part of a community is generally positive - people like to belong.
- But communities can also be challenging: members may differ on how things should be done, and tensions develop - as true for a football team as for a student council.

THE FIRST FOLLOWERS OF JESUS
- After the death and resurrection of Jesus, his followers gathered to remember him and his words.
- They became communities of faith, keeping the memory of Jesus alive.
- They supported one another as they tried to live as Jesus asked.
- Like all communities, they struggled with questions and tensions, but also enjoyed love and unity.

THE KINGDOM AND THE SECOND COMING
- As well as understanding who Jesus was, the early Christians struggled to understand what shape their mission should take.
- The coming of the Kingdom was central to Jesus’ teaching and influenced the early communities.
- In the years just after Jesus’ death and resurrection, his followers believed the Kingdom of God would come in their lifetime.
- Paul’s letter to the Thessalonians shows he believed he would be alive for the second coming:
- ‘For this we declare to you by the word of the Lord, that we who are alive, who are left until the coming of the Lord, will by no means precede those who have died.’ (1 Thessalonians 4:15)
- As time went on, Paul faced the reality that he would probably die before the Kingdom came.
- So the followers had to consider that the Kingdom might not be fully realised for a very long time.
- This played a significant part in shaping the Christian communities and, eventually, the Church.

INSTRUCTIONS AND NAMES
- Jesus gave clear instructions to his followers to continue after his death.
- He asked them to come together around a common meal in memory of him.
- They saw themselves as called in a very special way. Names they gave themselves: The Elect, The Chosen, The Saints.
- These names gave them a special status with Yahweh.
- They called themselves ‘Ekklesia’ (Jewish equivalent: ‘Kehal Yahweh’, the community of God).
- They saw themselves as an ESCHATOLOGICAL COMMUNITY - keeping Jesus’ message alive until the imminent coming of the Kingdom.

PAUL’S LETTERS AS THE SOURCE
- The chapter studies three communities founded by St Paul: Corinth, Philippi and Thessalonica.
- It looks at their issues, structure and organisation, and how they related to the Jesus movement of the time.
- The primary source is Paul’s letters to these churches, in which he responded to their issues.
- With no telephone, fax, computer or reliable transport, the letter was the central means of communication.
- While away, Paul gave support, guidance and advice through his letters.
- The communities faced great difficulties setting themselves up in the hostile environment after Jesus’ death.
- Paul’s letters give vital insight into their development.
- Acts 2:44-45: ‘All who believed were together and had all things in common; they would sell their possessions and goods and distribute the proceeds to all, as any had need.’

THE COMMUNITY AT PHILIPPI

FOUNDATION
- Believed to be the FIRST EUROPEAN Christian community founded by Paul.
- Probably founded on his SECOND missionary journey, around 49 or 50 CE.
- Acts tells how Paul and Silas met a Philippian woman named LYDIA, who was baptised with her family.
- Others in Philippi were impressed with Paul and Silas and formed the Church at Philippi.
- Paul and Silas were ordered by the city magistrates to leave Philippi (the textbook cites Acts 17:1-10). They went on to Thessalonica.

THE CITY
- A city of great importance in the Roman province of Macedonia, in north-eastern Greece.
- Population: Greeks, Macedonians and a small number of Jews.

LIFE OF THE COMMUNITY
- Convinced of the power of the message of Jesus Christ, like all communities of the time.
- Under Paul and others, it worked to witness to the message of love.
- Believers gathered in small groups for prayer, preaching and the breaking of bread.
- They cared for the weak and needy among them.
- This care extended to supporting Paul himself on his missionary journeys.
- This selfless love and mutual service embodied Jesus’ message of love of God and neighbour.

DIFFICULTIES AT PHILIPPI
- Persecution from many non-believing Gentiles - a Christian community growing in an alien environment.
- A new religion whose leader had been executed by the Romans was bound to cause trouble. Paul and Silas were asked to leave.
- Most members were Gentiles. Paul assured them that keeping Jewish laws was not required for membership.
- But some Jewish Christian missionaries urged them to keep basic Jewish laws, such as circumcision of male members. This caused tension.
- In his letter Paul explained circumcision was not required for non-Jews.
- Internal quarrelling between two prominent women, EUODIA and SYNTYCHE. Paul warned of the dangers of internal conflict and urged them to unite as members of one Church with one goal.

CHARACTERISTICS OF PHILIPPI
- The first European Christian community.
- Enthusiastic and joyful.
- A generous community.
- Some evidence of factions.
- Evidence of differing views on keeping Jewish laws.

THE COMMUNITY AT CORINTH

THE CITY
- A seaport at the southern tip of Macedonia (as the textbook puts it); a city of great importance in the ancient world.
- Part of the Roman Empire, attracting many cultures and traditions.
- Described as a ‘melting pot full of devotees of various pagan cults’.
- Very wealthy because of its commercial importance - but there was also poverty.
- The shape and problems of the Corinthian Church come from its wide variety of cultures and the differing economic status of its members.

FOUNDATION AND LETTERS
- Founded by Paul on his SECOND missionary journey in 51 CE.
- First letter to the Corinthians written in 56 CE; second letter in 57 CE.
- The Church was struggling to understand itself.
- The demands of this RADICAL FAITH were hard for many. Christianity called for love, sharing and unity - hard to live in a society so divided economically and culturally.
- The Church reflected many divisions present in the city.

PROBLEM 1: LOYALTY TO LEADERS (APOLLOS)
- Although founded by Paul, the community seems to have been more inspired by another preacher, APOLLOS.
- Members tended to identify with particular Christian leaders, which caused division. Paul warned them about this.

PROBLEM 2: MEAT SACRIFICED TO IDOLS
- The community came from a largely pagan environment.
- Some members were scandalised by eating meat sacrificed to pagan idols.
- Others thought the sacrifice meant nothing for Christians and saw no problem. This group thought they were more spiritually mature and looked down on the others.
- Paul advised them to follow their conscience and be sensitive to the conscience of others.
- 1 Corinthians 10:31-33: ‘…whether you eat or drink, or whatever you do, do everything for the glory of God. Give no offence to Jews or to Greeks or to the Church of God, just as I try to please everyone in everything I do, not seeking my own advantage, but that of many, so that they may be saved.’

PROBLEM 3: DIVISIONS AT LITURGICAL GATHERINGS
- Members were expected to show love and communion in daily life, especially at liturgical gatherings. But divisions in everyday life spilled over into worship.
- Head-dress: disagreement over whether the same rules applied to men and women about wearing head-dress at assemblies.
- Rich and poor: the wealthy ate and drank in abundance while the poor went without.
- Gifts of the Spirit: Paul had identified the gifts of the Spirit. Some thought some gifts were more valuable than others, leading to divisions and differences in status.
- All three show a community struggling with EQUALITY and UNITY - central to Jesus’ message.

PROBLEM 4: RESURRECTION OF THE BODY
- Some members did not believe in the resurrection of the dead.
- Paul said that if they did not believe in the resurrection of the dead, they did not believe in the resurrection of Jesus.
- Belief in the resurrection of Jesus was a requirement of their faith.

OTHER
- In his second letter Paul even refers to their lack of generosity.
- Still, the Church at Corinth did struggle to live out Jesus’ challenging message.

CHARACTERISTICS OF CORINTH
- A variety of cultures and traditions.
- Elitism and rivalry were problems.
- Paul’s authority was questioned by some.
- A tendency to marginalise the poor.
- Liturgical assemblies highlighted the divisions.

THE COMMUNITY AT THESSALONICA

FOUNDATION
- Founded by Paul during his SECOND missionary journey (Acts 17:1-14).
- Thessalonica was south of Philippi, in the Roman province of Macedonia.
- (1) Thessalonians was written around 50-51 CE. It is the EARLIEST individual part of the entire New Testament.

DIFFICULTIES AT THESSALONICA
- Persecution from some of their own countryfolk. They tried to live the ‘Good News’ despite this.
- GREATEST PROBLEM: expectation of the imminent return of Jesus.
- Some members began to ignore the commandments, thinking the end of the world was so near they might as well enjoy themselves.
- Paul urged them to be in a constant state of readiness through their faith, hope and love, and to act justly at all times.
- Their faith was not in doubt, but their behaviour left a lot to be desired.
- Some evidence that their sexual conduct was not what was expected of a follower of Jesus.
- 1 Thessalonians 4:4-5: ‘…that each one of you know how to control your own body in holiness and honour, not with lustful passion, like the Gentiles who do not know God.’
- Like Corinth, they struggled to hold on to belief in the resurrection of the dead. They worried about members who had already died.
- Paul emphasised the importance of belief in the Resurrection.

CHARACTERISTICS OF THESSALONICA
- Persecution from outside the community.
- Preoccupied with the imminent return of Jesus.
- Inclined to ignore the commandments about daily living.

QUICK COMPARISON
- Philippi: first in Europe, c. 49-50 CE, Lydia, generous and joyful, persecution by Gentiles, circumcision debate, Euodia and Syntyche.
- Corinth: 51 CE, letters 56 and 57 CE, wealthy seaport with poverty, Apollos, meat sacrificed to idols, head-dress, rich and poor, gifts of the Spirit, resurrection doubts.
- Thessalonica: second journey, letter c. 50-51 CE (earliest NT writing), persecution, imminent return of Jesus, ignoring commandments, sexual conduct, worry about the dead.

TEXTBOOK QUESTIONS, ASSIGNMENTS AND DISCUSSION
- Why do humans form groups? What groups do you belong to?
- Group work: community values in twenty-first-century Ireland - has consumerism banished real community?
- Questions on each city: what do you know about it, its characteristics, its main problems.
- Outline the issues that caused the greatest difficulties for the three communities.
- Choose one community and write about: its geographical location; its expressions of Christian belief; patterns of behaviour from this belief; difficulties within the community and with the wider culture.
- Reflection: problems facing the Church today and advice for faithful followers of Christ.

rows.prompt: According to the chapter, why do people naturally gather in groups after a shared experience?

To remember, celebrate and relive it

People who share the same job
People who speak the same language
People who share certain beliefs or interests

rows.prompt: Explain what the early Christians meant by calling themselves ‘Ekklesia’ and an ‘eschatological community’.
rows.model_answer: Ekklesia, like the Jewish ‘Kehal Yahweh’, means the community of God; for followers of the risen Jesus it meant the true community of God. Calling themselves an eschatological community meant they saw themselves as keeping Jesus’ message alive until the Kingdom of God came, which they expected very soon.

rows.prompt: How did the expected timing of the Kingdom of God change, and why did this matter?
rows.model_answer: At first the followers, including Paul (1 Thessalonians 4:15), believed the Kingdom would come in their lifetime. As time passed Paul realised he would probably die first, so they had to accept it might take a very long time. This played a major part in shaping the communities and eventually the Church.

rows.prompt: Why are Paul’s letters important for studying the first Christian communities?
rows.model_answer: They are the primary source for Corinth, Philippi and Thessalonica, because in them Paul responded to each community’s issues. With no reliable transport or other communication, letters let Paul give support, guidance and advice while away, and they give vital insight into how the communities developed.

rows.prompt: Describe how the community at Philippi lived out the message of Jesus.
rows.model_answer: Believers gathered in small groups for prayer, preaching and the breaking of bread. They cared for the weak and needy among them and even supported Paul on his missionary journeys. This selfless love and mutual service embodied Jesus’ message of love of God and neighbour.

rows.prompt: Name two difficulties experienced by the community at Philippi.
rows.model_answer: They suffered persecution from non-believing Gentiles, since theirs was a new religion whose leader had been executed by Rome. There was also tension when Jewish Christian missionaries urged circumcision of male members, and quarrelling between two women, Euodia and Syntyche.

rows.prompt: Why was there division within the Christian community at Corinth?
rows.model_answer: Corinth was a wealthy seaport with many cultures and pagan cults, but also poverty, and the Church reflected these divisions. Members identified with particular leaders such as Apollos, disagreed about eating meat sacrificed to idols, and divided at worship over head-dress, rich and poor, and the gifts of the Spirit.

rows.prompt: How did belief in the resurrection of the dead cause problems at Corinth and Thessalonica?
rows.model_answer: At Corinth some members did not believe in the resurrection of the dead, and Paul said this meant they did not believe in Jesus’ resurrection, which was required by their faith. At Thessalonica members struggled to keep this belief and worried about those who had already died, so Paul stressed the importance of belief in the Resurrection.

rows.prompt: Give three characteristics of the community at Thessalonica.
rows.model_answer: It experienced persecution from outside the community, from some of its own countryfolk. It was preoccupied with the imminent return of Jesus. It was inclined to ignore the commandments about daily living, including standards of sexual conduct.

rows.prompt: Choose one early Christian community you have studied (Corinth, Philippi or Thessalonica). Write an account of it under: (i) its geographical location; (ii) its expressions of Christian belief; (iii) the difficulties within the community and in relation to the wider culture.
rows.model_answer:
Corinth. (i) Corinth was a seaport at the southern tip of Macedonia, part of the Roman Empire. Because of its commercial importance it was very wealthy, though there was also poverty, and it attracted many cultures; it was called a ‘melting pot full of devotees of various pagan cults’. Paul founded the Church there on his second missionary journey in 51 CE and wrote letters to it in 56 and 57 CE.
(ii) Christianity was a radical faith calling for love, sharing and unity. Members were expected to show love and communion in daily life and especially at liturgical gatherings. Belief in the resurrection of Jesus was required.
(iii) The Church reflected the city’s divisions. Members identified with leaders, especially Apollos, causing rivalry, and some questioned Paul’s authority. Coming from a pagan background, they disagreed about eating meat sacrificed to idols; Paul told them to follow their conscience, respect others and ‘do everything for the glory of God’ (1 Corinthians 10:31). At worship they argued about head-dress, the rich ate and drank while the poor went without, and some ranked the gifts of the Spirit. Some denied the resurrection of the dead. Paul even mentioned their lack of generosity.
rows.marking_scheme: Three headings. (i) 5 marks: location, Roman Empire, wealth/poverty, cultures, foundation date. (ii) 5 marks: radical faith of love, sharing, unity; liturgical gatherings; resurrection belief. (iii) 10 marks: very good 8-10, good 5-7, fair 0-4 - Apollos/rivalry, Paul’s authority, meat sacrificed to idols and Paul’s advice, head-dress, rich and poor, gifts of the Spirit, resurrection doubts, lack of generosity. Equivalent points accepted for Philippi or Thessalonica.

rows.prompt: From your study of the early Christian communities at Corinth, Philippi and Thessalonica, outline the issues that caused the greatest difficulties for these communities.
rows.model_answer: At Philippi, the first European community, the members suffered persecution from non-believing Gentiles, because Christianity was a new religion whose leader had been executed by the Romans; Paul and Silas were even ordered out by the magistrates. Most members were Gentiles, but Jewish Christian missionaries urged circumcision of male members, which caused tension until Paul explained it was not needed for non-Jews. Two prominent women, Euodia and Syntyche, quarrelled, and Paul urged unity. At Corinth the Church reflected the city’s cultural and economic divisions. Members followed rival leaders such as Apollos, argued about eating meat sacrificed to idols, and divided at worship over head-dress, the gifts of the Spirit and the rich eating while the poor went hungry. Some denied the resurrection of the dead. At Thessalonica there was persecution from their countryfolk, but the greatest problem was expecting the imminent return of Jesus. Some ignored the commandments, including in sexual conduct, so Paul told them to control their bodies ‘in holiness and honour’ (1 Thessalonians 4:4) and to stay ready through faith, hope and love. They also worried about members who had died. Across all three, the struggle was to live Jesus’ message of love, equality and unity.
rows.marking_scheme: Very good 16-20, good 10-15, fair 0-9. At least two issues from each community for very good. May refer to: Philippi - persecution, circumcision, Euodia and Syntyche. Corinth - Apollos/factions, meat sacrificed to idols, head-dress, rich and poor, gifts of the Spirit, resurrection. Thessalonica - persecution, imminent return, ignoring commandments, sexual conduct, worry about the dead.

rows.prompt: What was the greatest problem experienced by the Thessalonian community, and how did Paul respond?
rows.model_answer: The Thessalonian Church was founded by Paul on his second missionary journey, and his letter to it (around 50-51 CE) is the earliest part of the New Testament. The community’s greatest problem came from expecting the imminent return of Jesus. Some members began to ignore the commandments, believing the end of the world was so near that they might as well enjoy themselves. There is also evidence their sexual conduct fell short of what was expected. Paul responded by urging them to be in a constant state of readiness through faith, hope and love, and to act justly at all times. He called on them to ‘control your own body in holiness and honour, not with lustful passion’ (1 Thessalonians 4:4-5). He also stressed the importance of belief in the Resurrection, since they worried about members who had already died.
rows.marking_scheme: Problem identified 2 marks; explained (ignoring commandments, enjoying themselves, sexual conduct) 3 marks. Paul’s response (readiness through faith, hope, love; act justly; 1 Thessalonians 4:4-5; Resurrection) 5 marks.

rows.prompt: Explain why the first followers of Jesus formed communities and how they understood themselves.
rows.model_answer: When people share an experience, they naturally gather to remember it, celebrate it and relive it. After the death and resurrection of Jesus, his followers gathered to remember him and his words. They became communities of faith, keeping his memory alive and supporting one another as they tried to live as he asked. Jesus had told them to come together around a common meal in memory of him. They saw themselves as specially called, naming themselves The Elect, The Chosen and The Saints, which gave them a special status with Yahweh. They called themselves ‘Ekklesia’, the true community of God (in Jewish terms ‘Kehal Yahweh’). They were an eschatological community, keeping Jesus’ message alive until the Kingdom of God, which they expected very soon.
rows.marking_scheme: Why communities formed (to remember, celebrate, support; Jesus’ instruction about a common meal) 4 marks. Self-understanding (Elect, Chosen, Saints; Ekklesia/Kehal Yahweh; eschatological community) 6 marks.
